comparedAgainst: GeeksforGeeks, Normal Forms in DBMS (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/normal-forms-in-dbms/): fetched. Uses isolated, non-evolving toy examples per normal form (a Phone Numbers column for 1NF, a bare (StudentID, CourseID, StudentName) sketch for 2NF, (StudentID, CourseID, Instructor) for 3NF/BCNF). No single denormalized table carried through all four forms, no runnable SQL, no anomaly demonstrated with an actual INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, no exercises.

Guru99, Database Normalization in SQL (https://www.guru99.com/database-normalization.html): fetched. Uses a video-rental-library example (member name/address/salutation, a multi-valued Movies Rented column) carried through 1NF-3NF; BCNF gets one sentence and no worked example ('sometimes called 3.5NF'). No runnable code, no functional-dependency formalism, no exercises, no engine-specific behavior.

Wikipedia, Boyce-Codd normal form (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyce%E2%80%93Codd_normal_form): fetched. Uses a tennis-court-booking table (Court, Start time, End time, Rate type) and a nearest-shop table for its BCNF counterexamples; no SQL, no anomaly demonstrations, no exercises, no connection to 1NF/2NF/3NF in one running example.

Sources spot-checked, not competitors: Silberschatz/Korth/Sudarshan Database System Concepts 7th ed. ch.7 slides (PDF fetched and text-extracted with pdftotext) and Ramakrishnan/Gehrke Database Management Systems 3rd ed. ch.19 slides (same); sqlite.org lang_altertable.html, datatype3.html and stricttables.html (all fetched).
justification: Judged as a Google low-value-content reviewer, this page is the opposite of thin, templated or copied, and it decisively outperforms the pages that actually rank for 'database normalization' or 'BCNF example'. GeeksforGeeks and Wikipedia use disconnected toy fragments with no runnable code; Guru99 carries one example through 1NF-3NF but waves at BCNF in a sentence. This article runs a single messy table (order_flat, a bookstore's orders/customers/products/reps) through every anomaly and every normal form with real SQL: the update, insertion and deletion anomalies in the second section are each produced by an actual INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE against real rows and a real error message, not asserted, satisfying the requirement that no anomaly is claimed without a demonstration; the BCNF section goes further than any of the three competitors checked by proving both dependencies of rep_of with GROUP BY/HAVING queries against the live data rather than stipulating them. run-code.mjs confirms PASS, blocks=54, executed=30, matching what the article claims runs. Originality check: the order_flat bookstore schema (customers, products, salespeople with a one-rep-per-customer-per-category rule) matches none of the three fetched competitors' examples, and I did not find it in any DBMS course material I could reach. The BCNF-specific rep_of/salesperson_id relation is structurally isomorphic to the field's canonical minimal BCNF counterexample -- I pulled the actual Silberschatz ch.7 PDF text and confirmed its dept_advisor(s_ID, i_ID, dept_name) example uses exactly the same functional-dependency skeleton (a determinant that is prime but not a superkey, paired with a two-attribute superkey that overlaps it) that rep_of(customer_id, product_category, salesperson_id) uses. That skeleton (three attributes, two overlapping candidate keys, one exception 3NF grants and BCNF does not) is the standard minimal shape needed to demonstrate this specific normal-form gap and recurs across essentially every DB course under different names; the entities, column names, data, narrative and business domain here are entirely the writer's own, so this reads as legitimate reuse of an unavoidable mathematical pattern, not a reskinned textbook example, and it does not cross the 'do not reuse a source's running example' line. Citations spot-checked against the primary documents (not just trusted): I fetched and PDF-extracted both slide decks. Silberschatz's own functional-dependency definition ('whenever any two tuples t1 and t2 of r agree on the attributes alpha, they also agree on the attributes beta') matches what the article attributes to it; Ramakrishnan and Gehrke's anomaly discussion does use a different running example (Hourly_Emps), exactly as the article says when it cites them; the sqlite.org DROP COLUMN restrictions, the INTEGER-affinity zip-code claim, and the STRICT-tables-since-3.37.0 claim are all verified accurate against the live pages. No filler: the opening sentence states a concrete scenario, there is no restated title, no 'in this article', no summary-of-headings conclusion (the final paragraph adds a genuine synthesizing point about the four forms rather than recapping section titles). No ad code. Structure reads nothing like its two pillar siblings: headings ('Three ways the flat table corrupts itself', 'The redundancy 3NF didn't catch') are content-specific, not boilerplate, and unlike sql-joins' round-1 draft, exercises are placed mid-article at the point they fit, are not gathered under a final 'Exercises' heading, and none leaks its answer outside the collapsed :::solution (checked all three: 'A column that snuck back in', 'Same shape, a different business', 'Build the reporting table'). docs/crosslinks/databases/normalization.md exists with sensible, specific pending links (indexes, transactions-and-acid) and explicit boundary notes with the two published siblings, so the brief's exemption for unpublished-sibling links applies cleanly, unlike sql-joins' round-1 draft which had no such file. Two sourcing gaps keep this off a 9+: 'Codd's original description of the relational model required exactly this [atomicity]' is a specific, named factual claim with no citation anywhere near it, and Codd's paper is not even in this article's own source list (the sibling relational-model-and-keys article already cites Codd's 1970 paper for the identical atomicity claim, and this article's own Silberschatz source covers 1NF/atomicity too, per its ch.7 slide section 'Atomic Domains and First Normal Form' that I confirmed exists in the fetched PDF); and the front-matter source 'SQLite: CREATE TABLE (composite PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL)' (lang_createtable.html) is never linked or referenced anywhere in the body -- grepping every URL in the file shows it appears only in front matter, an isolated instance of the padded-bibliography pattern the pilot lessons call out (the article's other five sources are each cited inline at least once). A smaller, non-blocking note: the toolchain sentence ('The SQL on this page runs on SQLite 3.37 or later ... results shown come from SQLite 3.50, with every statement run in order in one session') is close in both content and sentence shape to relational-model-and-keys' toolchain sentence ('The SQL runs on SQLite 3.37 or later; the results shown come from SQLite 3.50. Run the statements in order in one session.'); the underlying facts must appear on every page per the writer guide, but the phrasing echo across two of three live pillar siblings is worth varying further. None of this is a policy risk or a correctness error; together it is the difference between 'clearly better, no notes' and 'MDN-quality with real, fixable nits'.
